extracted.intended_audience: landscape painters, art students, and art critics interested in truthful rendering of sky, light, mist, and earth (readers of Ruskin/Turner criticism)
extracted.subtask_short: rendering skies and light in landscape
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing and evaluating landscape paintings with truthful representation of skies, clouds, mist, rain, light at different hours, and the bare earth's structure. Emphasizes perceptual truth, medium-appropriate technique, and avoidance of conventional/engraver's clichés.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sky colour gradation and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: The blue sky in openings should be shown as 'melting and palpitating colour, never the same for two inches together,' with clouds passing off in 'faint white threads and fringes' through which blue 'shines more and more intensely' until vapour is lost in perfect color; the upper white clouds become white as they disappear so that the blue is never 'corrupted' but only paled and broken with pure white.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for exquisite gradation and change rather than uniform flat blue. Avoid the old-master habit of a pool of stagnant blue bounded by sharp, imperturbable cloud edges. Examples: the delicate, dreamy blue passages in Turner, contrasted with the old masters' 'hole in the sky' approach; observe nature (first opening after rain) to test truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety and transparent edges of rain-clouds (near clouds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Near rain-clouds are characterised by 'loose and shattering transparency' and 'fragments of spray'—their loose, shattering transparency is essential; cloud-edges should show agreeable transparency and variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render edges as delicate and varied, not hard, opaque, or solid. Anti-pattern: Gaspar Poussin's wreaths of cloud with 'unpleasant edges cut as hard and solid and opaque and smooth as thick black paint', which read like 'a dirty sail badly reefed.' Good examples: Turner drawings where white rain gleams beneath dark transparent shadows, and cloud-edges that melt along hillsides (Oakhampton, Ben Lomond, Llanberis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mist and intermediate aerial effects must be immediately felt
rubrics_metrics.description: Aerial and misty effects are matters 'of which the eye should be simply cognizant... being exquisitely rendered, either be felt at once, or prove... blindness and bluntness in the feelings of the observer.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render mist so that its presence is perceived without analytical effort; if well done it should be felt instinctively as nature's light/diffusion. This requires accurate observation of phenomena like dew rising from pasture or storm gathering on a sea-cliff. Examples: Simmer Lake (mist pervaded with sunlight), Lake Lucerne (recession into luminous cloud), Harlech, Ehrenbreitstein, Oberwesel, Nemi.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of spontaneous brush-dash with considered form
rubrics_metrics.description: While a single brush-dash in watercolour can come nearer to the truth of rain-blue than a day of oil work, in Turner 'the dash of the brush is as completely under the rule of thought and feeling as its slowest line; all that it does is perfect, and could not be altered, even in a hairbreadth, without injury.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that apparently careless or rapid strokes are governed by deliberate thought and feeling; avoid accidental or unconsidered forms (as in some works by Tayler and Cox). Each mark must be intentional and integral to the composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of medium suited to atmospheric transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain atmospheric effects (the melting, dewy rain-blue) are sometimes better achieved by watercolour—'one accidental dash of the brush with water-colour on a piece of wet or damp paper, will come nearer the truth and transparency of this rain-blue than the labor of a day in oils.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select medium with awareness of its capacity for transparency and melting effects. Watercolour can produce felicitous, careless, melting skies (Cox, Tayler) but beware of unconsidered form; Turner achieves similar transparency in conjunction with considered drawing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recession into luminous cloud and distance modulation
rubrics_metrics.description: The most difficult thing in art is the 'recession of near mountain form, not into dark, but into luminous cloud' — rendering near forms melting into luminous atmosphere rather than simple dark silhouettes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model distance so that near mountain forms fade into luminous cloud rather than merely darkening; study works like the Lake Lucerne drawing and practice subtle modulation of tone and colour to suggest luminous recession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles for rendering storms and tempest (Turner's rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: The great principles for storm-drawing: angular outline, vastness and energy of form, infinity of gradation, and depth without blackness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When rendering violent storms, avoid mere roundness and blackness; use sharp, writhing folds, violent angles, and varied, lurid colours (sulphurous tones), and allow large gradations to create depth without resorting to solid black. Example: Turner's Stonehenge storm: 'forms are marked with violent angles... fantastic and fiery volumes... an awful life.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Engraver/translator anti‑patterns for storm/cloud effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Common (incorrect) translation principles used by engravers: 1) Where the drawing is gray, make the paper black. 2) Where the drawing is white, cover the page with zigzag lines. 3) Where the drawing has particularly tender tones, cross-hatch them. 4) Where any outline is particularly angular, make it round. 5) Where there are vertical reflections in water, express them with very distinct horizontal lines. 6) Where there is a passage of particular simplicity, treat it in sections. 7) Where there is anything intentionally concealed, make it out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider these seven items as a checklist of misinterpretations to avoid when translating subtle tonal and linear work into other media (especially engraving). They illustrate how mechanical, formulaic handling destroys Turner's subtleties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rendering of the 'rainy fringe' and suspended rain formations
rubrics_metrics.description: The rainy 'fringe' — rain-clouds in distances that do not reach the earth but are 'suspended in waving and twisted lines from the darkness of the zenith' — must be indicated as suspended waving and twisted lines, or as a 'rainy fringe' cutting the sky into regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict distant rain as suspended veils or fringes that admit varied visibility of the plain beneath (as in Waterloo, Richmond, Dunstaffnage, Glencoe, St. Michael's Mount, Slave Ship). Avoid showing rain as a solid mass reaching the ground when the natural phenomenon is a suspended veil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate depiction of light specific to hour and direction
rubrics_metrics.description: Light effects vary markedly by hour and direction (front light, lateral light, lateral-front, lateral-behind). Turner catalogues distinct classes of effects for Morning, Noon/Afternoon, Evening, and Night—each combination of time, weather, and light direction produces distinctive skies and lighting to be rendered truthfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a systematic classification of light by time-of-day and sun direction (Ruskin's prefixed letters F, L, L.F., L.B.) when planning or evaluating a picture. Refer to the catalogue (e.g., 'sunrise with misty cirri' => Alps at Daybreak; 'afternoon after rain with descending sunbeams' => Carew Castle) as illustrative exemplars. Ensure the painting's lighting matches observable physical conditions for the specified hour and weather.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth of earth: faithful representation of ground anatomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth of earth means the faithful representation of the facts and forms of the bare ground, divested of vegetation. Ground is to the landscape painter what the naked human body is to the historical painter; the laws of the organisation of the earth are distinct, fixed, and foundational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the structure of the earth as the foundation of landscape composition. Know and respect the simple, broad laws that govern bare ground; ignorance or abandonment of these laws leads to deformity and falsehood in landscape painting. The earth's forms should be understood as modulating vegetation and water, not merely decorative background.
